messages.subject: Re: Modelling behavioral response
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm new to the oSCR package. I am interested in learning more about what kind of behavioral responses can be modelled. By the way, talking about data requirements,  the behavioral response must be operationalized as a discrete, continuous, ordinal variable (?). What kind of animal responses can be modeled?. There are there a couple of examples available to introduce myself to this sub-topic (2 papers)?

Thanks in advance!!!

Best, Victor ;)

El miércoles, 22 de noviembre de 2017, 19:10:02 (UTC+1), Daniel Linden escribió:
> Hi Jenni,
>
> The p.behav coefficient is for a trap-specific behavioral response, so the model is indicating that capture probability essentially goes to zero for a given individual at a given trap after initial capture.  The problem is that you did not observe an individual recaptured in the same trap.  I'm not sure there is a great fix for this.  If the behavioral response is real, you'd want to keep it in the model to adjust p0 (and subsequently, d0).  But the coefficient will have a nonsense estimate because of the link scale conversion of Pr(y = 1) = 0, which is negative infinity.
>
> What kind of traps were used?  If they were live-capture traps, you'd want to make sure the multinomial model (multicatch = T) is used.
>

messages.subject: caution: be careful using a local state-space definition (trimS option in oSCR) when you have spatial covariates on detection
messages.subject_clean: caution: be careful using a local state-space definition (trimS option in oSCR) when you have spatial covariates on detection
messages.body_plain:
Dear SCR users,

 Our package oSCR has an option to do a local state-space evaluation of the likelihood (trimS = ) where normally if you set trimS to be about 2-3 x the parameter 'sigma' of the half-normal detection model you obtain the same result as if you evaluated the likelihood over the full state-space (and it saves a lot of computing time).  I've also seen people do this kind of local state-space definition with Bayesian analysis in WinBUGS or JAGS too.  I imagine that Efford's package SECR also does this but I'm not sure.

 In any case, the recommended choice for trimS of 2-3 x 'sigma' is based on a detection model that is only a function of distance, and it ensures that detection probability is near 0 at the edge of the local state-space.  However, when there are spatial covariates modeled on detection probability (e.g., habitat type) then it's not generally possible to pick a value of trimS to ensure a near-0 detection probability. Indeed, it will depend on the specific covariates used in the model, and their values at the traps.

 Therefore: when you have spatial covariates on detection probability you SHOULD NOT USE trimS or, in general, should not use a local definition of the state-space.

regards
andy
